questions.q: What is the export-then-visualize pattern this lesson describes?
options: A PowerShell script collects metrics on a schedule and writes them to a structured source; a separate dashboard tool reads that source and renders it
A PowerShell script renders its own charts directly in the console
SQL Server Agent automatically builds dashboards with no scripting involved
Metrics are only ever viewed by manually running a query each time
questions.explain: The pattern deliberately separates collecting data (the script's job) from visualizing it (the dashboard tool's job).

questions.q: What does `Export-Csv -Append` accomplish across repeated scheduled runs of the metrics script?
options: It appends a new row each run, building up a real time series in the CSV over time
It overwrites the entire file every time, keeping only the latest row
It deletes the CSV file after each run
It only works the first time the script ever runs
questions.explain: Appending rather than overwriting is what turns individual runs into a genuine time series.

questions.q: Which real tools does the lesson name as ones that can read metrics a script exports?
options: Power BI and Grafana
SQL Server Agent and dbatools
Terraform and Bicep
MailKit and Send-MailMessage
questions.explain: Power BI and Grafana are named as real, widely used dashboard tools that connect to the exported data source.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the PowerShell script's job should stop at writing the data, rather than also rendering a UI?
options: Because that's outside what a script is good at — dashboarding, charting, and refresh scheduling are what a dedicated dashboard tool is built for
Because PowerShell cannot technically write to a CSV file
Because Power BI and Grafana cannot read from CSV or SQL Server sources
Because rendering a UI in PowerShell is against Microsoft's licensing terms
questions.explain: The lesson's honest framing is a clean division of labor: collection belongs to the script, visualization belongs to the dashboard tool.

questions.q: Per the lesson's honest caveat, when should a team move past this export-then-visualize pattern to a dedicated monitoring platform?
options: When they need real alerting rules, long retention, and reliable collection from many hosts at scale
Never — this pattern scales to any size team without limitation
As soon as they have more than one SQL Server instance
Only if Power BI is unavailable in their organization
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this is a good fit for a small team without a full platform's needs, not a permanent substitute at scale.
